title: The clever sage
hookLine: Mahosadha solves the court's riddles and saves the kingdom by wit (Jataka 546)

cards: Two women, one baby, and a judge who is still a child. Each woman swears the baby is hers. Nobody saw what happened.
In the Jataka the judge is a village boy named Mahosadha, who has built a hall where people bring their quarrels, and this is one of them. He doesn't ask for witnesses. He draws a line on the ground.

teach.b: The story says he was born holding a healing herb, and so he was called Mahosadha, great medicine: a fitting name for someone whose gift is fixing things. Back to the line.
He places the baby on it and tells the women to pull, one by the arms, one by the legs; whoever pulls the child across keeps him. They pull. The baby cries out.
And one woman lets go, rather than hurt him. That, the boy says, is the mother. The other, the story reveals, wasn't human at all.
Case after case goes like that: he finds the answer by watching how people act, not by guessing. Word reaches King Vedeha of Mithila, who brings the boy to court.
There, jealous advisers test him, scheme against him, try to get him thrown out.
He keeps answering riddles, keeps seeing through traps.

teach.h: A GREAT TUNNEL SAVES THE KING.
teach.b: When a rival king threatens Mithila, Mahosadha's plan, a great tunnel, the ummagga the tale is named for, turns a trap into a peace and saves his king. Tradition pairs this tale with wisdom, panna.
It's a practical wisdom. It reads people, and it's always used to protect someone: the baby, the cheated, the king. The baby goes home with the woman who let go.

how: The Mahosadha story is told as a tale of practical wisdom; in Buddhist teaching, wisdom (panna) is one of the ten perfections.

o: a riddle set by a judge

games.q: who did what in Mahosadha's story: tap the pairs.
p: let go rather than hurt the baby
saved the king and made peace

s: the true mother was the one who pulled hardest
she let go rather than hurt the child, and Mahosadha knew her by that.
the story says he was born holding a healing herb
and so he was named Mahosadha, great medicine.
he watched how people acted and let their actions show the answer.

games.q: you're the boy judge. two women each claim the baby, and no one saw what happened. what do you do?
o: give the baby to the one who cries hardest.
set a test that shows who loves the child.
send them away to the king.
games.why: he has them pull the child across a line; the true mother lets go rather than hurt him.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose mood you've been guessing at lately, a child, a coworker, a friend who's gone quiet.

Set the guesses aside and recall only what they actually did this week, what they reached for and when they lit up, and let their actions tell you something, the way the mother's letting go told Mahosadha.

wordCard.voice: Panna. Wisdom: what Mahosadha the boy judge showed, reading people well and using his wit to protect them, all the way to saving his king. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali panna, wisdom: the perfection tradition pairs with Mahosadha's tale.

carryVoice: Your line: wit that saves. His cleverness always worked for someone else. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Jataka 546 (Mahaummagga Jataka, the tale of Mahosadha)
